title: Benchmark Report Copy v1 (working draft) — Latency per Dollar (Production Economics)
content:
Doc purpose: early draft copy for the public benchmark report (web + PDF). This is intentionally rough / iterative.

Primary goal of the report:
- Make “production economics” concrete for engineers AND procurement: latency per dollar (latency/$) with supporting throughput and cost metrics.
- Establish Redwood as a credible reference (repeatable methodology + constraints).

NOTE: This draft does not include final numbers. We’ll paste in headline stats once QC sign-off is final.

============================
0) Working titles / headline options
============================
Option A (straight):
- “The Redwood Production Economics Benchmark: Latency per Dollar Across Models and Regions”

Option B (engineer-friendly):
- “Latency/$ for LLM Inference: A Reproducible Benchmark Across Regions”

Option C (slightly more provocative, check claims policy):
- “Stop Optimizing for Tokens/$ Alone: Measuring Latency per Dollar in Production”

[Comment - Soojin]: Title needs to say “open models” somewhere without over-indexing on “open source vs closed.” Maybe: “Popular Open Models” or “Open-weight models.”

[Comment - Camila]: Avoid anything that reads like “we invented the metric.” We can say “we’re publishing a benchmark focused on…”

============================
1) TL;DR / Executive summary (draft)
============================
Teams aren’t choosing LLMs based on quality alone anymore. In production, the economics are driven by three things at once:
- How fast the model responds (latency)
- How much you can serve at steady load (throughput)
- What it costs to do it (cost per token / per request)

This report introduces a reproducible way to compare “production economics” across model families and cloud regions using a single metric: latency per dollar (latency/$), supported by p50/p95 latency, throughput, and cost.

We ran the benchmark across:
- Workloads: chat generation + embeddings baseline
- Regions: North America + Europe + at least one APAC region (final list in the table)
- A curated set of popular open-weight model families (final list in the table)

What you’ll get:
- A region-by-region view of latency/$ (and why region matters)
- A methodology appendix with enough detail to interpret results responsibly
- Practical guidance on how to apply these results to your own workload (and how to reproduce a smaller-scale version)

[Comment - Ben]: In the summary we should add one sentence about actions: “use this to choose model/region/deployment mode.” Keep it concrete.

============================
2) Intro / Why we wrote this
============================
When you ship LLM features into a real product, the “best” model is the one that meets your quality bar while staying inside your latency SLO and budget.

In practice, teams hit the same friction points:
- A model that looks cost-effective on a per-token basis can miss your p95 latency target at peak concurrency.
- The same model behaves differently across regions due to hardware availability, network distance, and capacity management.
- Benchmarks that report only throughput (or only single-stream latency) don’t reflect production tradeoffs.

So we built and are publishing a benchmark focused on a simple question:

“What is the latency you get per dollar spent, for a realistic production workload, in each region?”

This isn’t meant to be the final word for every workload. It is meant to be:
- Clear about assumptions
- Comparable across regions and models
- Reproducible (with guardrails)

[Comment - Jonas]: Please add a line acknowledging quality differences across models. Otherwise it reads like the only axis is economics.

Draft add:
Of course, economics only matter after you pick a model that meets your quality bar. This report focuses on the serving-side performance and cost tradeoffs once you’re comparing models that are “good enough” for your use case.

============================
3) Metric definition (plain English)
============================
Latency per dollar (latency/$) is a production-economics metric that combines:
- Latency (how long requests take) and
- Cost (how much you pay to serve them)

Intuition:
- Lower latency is better.
- Lower cost is better.
- Latency/$ tells you how much latency you’re “buying” for each dollar under a defined workload.

We report latency/$ alongside:
- p50 and p95 end-to-end latency
- Throughput (tokens/sec, requests/sec depending on workload)
- Cost per 1M tokens (or equivalent unit for embeddings)

[Comment - Sana]: Avoid saying “combines” if we’re worried about people assuming it’s a magical composite score. Better: “derived metric computed from measured latency and measured cost under the benchmark workload.”

Draft tweak:
Latency/$ is a derived metric computed from measured latency and measured cost under the benchmark workload.

============================
4) Methodology summary (short, for main body)
============================
We designed the benchmark to match common production patterns:

Workloads
1) Chat generation (streaming where supported)
- A prompt distribution representing typical app usage (short + medium + long context)
- A response length distribution (short answers + multi-paragraph)

2) Embeddings baseline
- Fixed-size inputs sampled from a representative distribution

Concurrency and load
- Requests are issued at controlled concurrency levels to simulate steady production traffic.
- We measure in a fixed window after warmup.

Warmup + caching policy
- We include a warmup period to avoid cold-start artifacts.
- Caching policy is explicitly defined (what is warmed, what is not). We do NOT rely on “mystery cache hits” to inflate numbers.

Measurement + repetition
- Each model/region configuration is run multiple times.
- We report summary stats and track run-to-run variance.
- If variance exceeds the rerun threshold, we rerun and/or investigate infra noise per the anomaly triage playbook.

Cost attribution
- Costs are derived from metered usage and the pricing assumptions documented in the appendix.
- We avoid using customer traffic or customer-identifying traces.

Guardrails
- Benchmarks are run in scheduled capacity windows with monitoring so they don’t impact production SLOs.

[Comment - Claire]: “We do NOT rely on mystery cache hits” is good but maybe too snarky for final. Keep in v1 but we’ll tone down.

[Comment - Wei]: For the PDF we should have a “Methodology in one page” that’s skimmable, then link to full appendix.

============================
5) Findings (narrative copy with placeholders)
============================
We’ll present results by region, because region is one of the biggest drivers of real-world user experience and cost.

5.1 Region matters more than most teams expect
Across model families, we see meaningful differences in both latency and latency/$ between regions.

Why this happens (non-exhaustive):
- Network distance to users
- Hardware mix and availability by region
- Capacity headroom and autoscaling behavior
- Background contention and noisy-neighbor effects (we control for this where possible)

Placeholder (insert chart callout):
- Figure 1: “Latency/$ by region (normalized)”

[TODO: Insert one safe headline stat with variance language]
Example structure (do not publish as-is):
- “In our runs, median latency/$ differed by ~X–Y% between Region A and Region B for the same model family (with run-to-run variance within Z%).”

[Comment - Michael (Legal/claims)]: If we use % differences, we must also state the benchmark workload + config and avoid “for the same model” unless it’s literally identical runtime/hardware assumptions. Add “under our benchmark configuration.”

5.2 Different model families land differently on the latency vs cost curve
Some model families are optimized for:
- Lower latency at moderate throughput
Others for:
- Higher throughput at the expense of tail latency

Latency/$ surfaces these tradeoffs clearly: a model can be “cheap” and still not be cost-effective if it forces you to overprovision to meet p95.

Placeholder chart callouts:
- Figure 2: “p95 latency vs cost per 1M tokens (scatter) by region”
- Figure 3: “Latency/$ ranking table (top N per region)”

[Comment - Markus]: Add one paragraph for SEs: “How to talk about this with engineers.” Specifically: “If your p95 is above SLO, throughput doesn’t matter.”

Draft paragraph:
If your application has a hard latency SLO, especially at p95, raw throughput numbers can be misleading. A configuration that looks “efficient” in tokens/sec may still drive higher all-in costs if you have to scale out aggressively to pull p95 below your SLO.

5.3 Variance and confidence: what’s stable vs what’s noisy
We observed that some configurations are highly stable run-to-run, while others show larger variance due to:
- Capacity headroom differences
- Sensitivity to batching behavior at specific sequence lengths
- Region-level background load

How to use this:
- Treat small differences within the variance band as “effectively tied.”
- Use the benchmark to narrow your shortlist, then validate with your workload.

Placeholder appendix reference:
- “See Appendix C: Variance, rerun policy, and how to interpret close results.”

[Comment - Sana]: We should explicitly state what we consider “close.” E.g., “within X%” but only after we confirm across all runs.

5.4 What this means for buying decisions
For engineering:
- Start with a quality-qualified model shortlist.
- Pick a region close to your users.
- Use latency/$ plus p95 latency to pick the best operational configuration.

For procurement / finance:
- Latency/$ expresses the tradeoff between user experience and spend in one number.
- It also makes “hidden scale costs” visible when tail latency forces overprovisioning.

[Comment - Jordan]: Add a sentence about deployment mode: hosted vs dedicated vs private. “If you need predictable throughput, dedicated changes the variance story.”

Draft add:
Deployment mode matters. Dedicated capacity can reduce variance and improve predictability for steady high-throughput workloads; Private deployments can be required for data residency and regulated environments. The benchmark results here are reported per region, with notes on how to translate the findings to Dedicated/Private evaluations.

============================
6) How to reproduce (short copy stub)
============================
You should be able to reproduce a smaller-scale version of this benchmark against your own prompts.

We provide:
- A minimal reproduction example (config + runner)
- A set of guidance on concurrency, warmup, and measurement windows

Important:
- Don’t compare your results to ours if your workload distribution is materially different.
- If you change caching/batching settings, document it (those levers matter).

[TODO: Link to reproduction example once merged]

============================
7) Calls to action (CTA variants)
============================
CTA set 1 (self-serve / PLG):
- “Try Redwood Hosted API (free credits) — measure latency/$ on your own traffic.”
- “Run the reproduction harness against your prompt set.”

CTA set 2 (sales-assisted / Dedicated):
- “Need predictable throughput? Talk to us about Dedicated capacity in your region.”
- “Share your latency SLO + traffic profile — we’ll recommend a configuration.”

CTA set 3 (regulated / Private):
- “Deploy in your VPC or on-prem — ask about Redwood Private.”
- “Security & compliance package available (SSO, audit logs, retention controls).”

CTA set 4 (comparison / eval angle):
- “Have an existing provider? Bring your traces (sanitized) and we’ll help you run an apples-to-apples evaluation.”

[Comment - Ben]: Each CTA needs one matching “micro-proof” line near it (e.g., “Dedicated: SLA + isolation” / “Private: VPC/on-prem + KMS/HSM”).

Draft micro-proof lines:
- Hosted API: “Fastest path to production; unified SDKs; streaming + tool calling.”
- Dedicated: “Reserved GPU pools, predictable throughput, data isolation, SLA options.”
- Private: “Customer-managed networking, audit logs, key management integrations.”

============================
8) Disclosures / constraints (must-have section; draft)
============================
This report is designed to be useful and credible, not overly absolute.

Key constraints to understand:
- Results depend on the benchmark workload definition (prompt lengths, response lengths, concurrency).
- Results are reported by region; region-to-region differences are expected.
- Small numerical differences may not be meaningful if they are within observed variance.
- The benchmark does not measure model quality. You should validate quality for your task.

We do not publish:
- Raw per-request logs
- Customer-identifying traces

[Comment - Michael]: Add a single line: “All trademarks belong to their respective owners.” Standard.

Add:
All trademarks and model names belong to their respective owners.

============================
9) Copy blocks for landing page / PDF reuse (grab-and-go)
============================
9.1 One-liner (internal + external)
“Redwood Inference is a developer-first platform for running and optimizing LLM inference across hosted, dedicated, and private deployments.”

9.2 What is “production economics” (short)
Production economics is the measurable tradeoff between latency, throughput, and cost when serving real workloads under load.

9.3 What is latency/$ (short)
Latency/$ is a derived metric computed from measured latency and measured cost under a defined workload, designed to make production tradeoffs easier to compare.

============================
10) Open questions / TODOs
============================
- Confirm final region naming convention for public tables (e.g., “us-east”, “eu-west”, “ap-southeast”) vs cloud-provider labels.
- Decide how many model families to include in the main report vs appendix.
- Decide whether to show absolute cost numbers or index/normalize (Marketing preference: show absolute + methodology appendix).
- Confirm claims language + “acceptable comparisons” checklist sign-off.
- Insert final headline findings (with variance/confidence language) once QC is complete.

============================
11) Reviewer notes (running)
============================
[Comment - Tessa]: For the PDF, we need 1–2 “interpretation callout” boxes (“How to read this chart”) so engineers don’t misread rankings.

[Comment - Wei]: If we publish a methodology appendix, the landing page should include 3 bullets max + link. Don’t dump detail above the fold.

[Comment - Claire]: Please avoid saying “apples-to-apples” unless we explicitly list the apples (same workload, same measurement window, same caching policy, etc.).

[Comment - Jonas]: Add line: “We welcome reproductions and critique.” It strengthens credibility.

Draft add (somewhere near the methodology section):
We welcome reproductions, feedback, and critique. If you find an issue or want to suggest a workload variant, contact us and we’ll incorporate it into the next refresh.
